en: The Second Contemplation of the Realm of Afflictions, as spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty and recorded by his disciple Guanding:
Regarding the aforementioned aggregates, realms, and bases (*skandha-dhātv-āyatana*), if one does not awaken to them, they are not [the true realm].
One should observe this continuously and repeatedly.
When afflictions such as greed and hatred are provoked and arise,
at that time one should abandon the contemplation of the aggregates and sense bases and instead contemplate the afflictions themselves.
First, one censures the five desires to recognize their faults and transgressions;
then, by abandoning the hindrances, one relinquishes the ordinary aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*);
finally, one contemplates the retributive fruits and seeks liberation therein.
Now, observe how when [the mind] is activated and becomes intense, it gives rise to strong greed and hatred;
it is like iron that remains black when not in contact with fire,
but blazes forth when in contact with fire.
Furthermore, regarding the nature of retribution, it is always easy to rebuke and abandon [unwholesome states] when they are habitual and constantly present;
however, if afflictions suddenly arise, it is difficult to control them. Why is this?
Although he has been prone to anger since birth, it would subside upon being admonished and enlightened;
yet what he has now unleashed is a raging fury, truly terrifying.
Furthermore, his lifelong inverted perceptions arise and vanish in sudden flashes.
What has now been aroused is surging and will not depart.
Desires for form and sensation that have arisen since birth can be suppressed and halted;
but what has now been aroused does not spare even a dead horse, let alone its peers.
These afflictions arise within with such force and intensity that,
when one perceives external objects, the mind becomes deranged and the vision darkened;
it is like flowing water whose rapidity goes unnoticed.
To generalize, it is like ripples rising upon wood;
it is also like a strong man who, unaware of his own strength, feels no anger when touched by something powerful.
Thus, the afflictions lie dormant, as if they were present and yet as if they were non-existent.
In the place of practice, one contemplates the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
This is like touching a sleeping lion that then roars and shakes the earth;
if one does not recognize it, it can drag one away to commit grave and heavy sins.
Not only will śamatha and vipaśyanā fail to be accomplished, but one’s evil karma will further increase;
one will fall into the pit of darkness from which there is no means of escape.
For this reason, one must contemplate the objects of the afflictions.
Contemplating this as fourfold:
first, a brief clarification of its characteristics;
second, clarifying its causes and conditions; third, [clarifying] its integration; and fourth, clarifying its distinctions.
Fourth, the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
First, regarding the characteristics,
we shall first explain the names.
Afflictions (*kleśa*) are phenomena that are dark and vexing, which disturb and confuse the mind.
Furthermore, they create vexation for the mind, causing it to experience distress.
These are precisely the sharp and dull aspects of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi* and *saṃjñā*).
This is a provisional classification.
Why must the five dull faculties necessarily be greed and hatred?
For instance, wriggling insects truly do not engage in rational inference.
Yet you lift your head, spread your fins, and glare with eyes of arrogance;
how could those base and inferior beings below ever harbor such views?
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they constantly give rise to the notion of a self.
Therefore, we know that the five dull [afflictions] are not without their sharp counterparts.
How could the five sharp [afflictions] consist of nothing but delusions of view?
When have they ever been devoid of anger and desire?
One should know that the designations "sharp" and "dull" apply generally to both the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).
Now, they are distinguished according to their stages so as not to be confused.
Prior to the arousal of dhyāna, although one may possess worldly wisdom, logical inference, eloquence, and sharp discernment, these perceptions remain weak.
All ten proclivities (anuśaya) belonging to the dull category arise determinately from their causes;
because the mind of speculative view (dṛṣṭi) is intense,
all ten proclivities that receive their names from being strong are classified as sharp (tīkṣṇa).
It is like two students: if one who has attained the meaning of the Dharma disputes with another who has merely mastered the words, the former is strong while the latter is weak.
Mastering the words is like being without meditation; attaining the meaning is like emerging from meditative concentration.
If one has already entered meditative concentration and gives rise to afflictions of view as observed below,
that is not the case here; rather, it is precisely when afflictions arise without having entered meditative concentration that this present observation applies.
If there were dullness within sharpness,
then even when one has seen the truths (dṛṣṭasatya) and severed the sharp [afflictions], the dull [afflictions] would still remain.
The Abhidharmikas maintain that the dullness existing upon the sharp is called the "latent tendency on the back" (pṛṣṭha-anuśaya).

When the truths are realized (*satyadarśana-prahāṇa*), the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) are eliminated, and their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are likewise eliminated; the same applies to the afflictions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa*).
If these [afflictions] were categorized according to their sharpness or dullness, they would amount to eighty-four thousand;
however, for now, they are simply condensed into four categories.
The three poisons manifest predominantly as the three divisions.
If they take the three objects equally as their conditions, it is called "equal parts" (sabhāga).
When the three poisons arise predominantly, this refers to vitarka and vicāra rather than to the many [defilements].
The arising of the three poisons and so forth is called "much vitarka and vicāra.

Whether slight or great, all such states are termed "distraction" (*vikṣepa*) and are capable of obstructing meditative concentration (*samādhi*). They are neutral (*avyākṛta*) and constitute retribution-based distraction (*vipākavikṣepa*), which does not obstruct concentration. As the Sūtra says:
One enters and emerges from the attainment of cessation into the state of distracted mind,
and from the state of distracted mind returns to various meditative attainments.
That "distraction does not obstruct meditative attainment" is precisely this meaning.
The *Abhidharmakośa* scholars say:
"If distraction is associated with both ignorance and delusion, and is thus able to obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
then why does distraction associated with both hatred and desire not likewise obstruct concentration?"
Now, the specific meaning has been explained above in the section on abandoning the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
However, the characteristics of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are so vast that they cannot be fully exhausted;
if they were analyzed in detail here, it would obstruct the gateway of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*).
The Lotus Sūtra says:
"For twenty years, he was constantly made to remove dung.
Dung refers to the defilements and impurities of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
If one discards them as if they were exhausted, one may obtain the price for a single day;
yet if one dwells upon discriminating between their quantity, one will ultimately never obtain the value.
Now, observe how one seeks the coin of wisdom within the filth of afflictions.
This is not to say that one discriminates between the characteristics of views and thoughts. If that were so,
why would the five hundred arhats have made such distinctions?
To uphold the Buddha-dharma and act as a leader for the multitude, one must master various difficult points through extensive analysis; however,
at this moment, I lack the leisure due to my entry into the power of the Path,
and such analysis is not urgent for my current contemplation.
One should simply know in general that there are four parts of impure filth and diligently discard them.
When entering the provisional from the empty, one should distinguish them with complete detail.
Furthermore, both the sharp and dull faculties are each grouped together into four parts.
Those that are abandoned by both [Bodhisattvas and] the Two Vehicles within the same realm are called pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).
Those that are not abandoned by the Two Vehicles in the four divisions outside the realm are called specific afflictions (*asādhāraṇa-kleśa*).
If they were related [to one another], how could there be specific afflictions apart from the pervasive ones?
The pervasive afflictions serve as the branches and the specific afflictions serve as the root.
One attains true wisdom to sever the branches and middle wisdom to sever the root.
If one acts with inconceivability, [the branches and root are severed].
The afflictions within the realm of *dharmadhātu* are themselves bodhi.
How could they not be distinct delusions?
This has already been explained as before.
Second, the causes and conditions for the arising of afflictions are explained.
There are three such causes and conditions, as will be described later;
there are four aspects of their arising.
"Deep but not sharp; sharp but not deep; both deep and sharp;
neither deep nor sharp. The fourth phrase pertains to the characteristics of the delusions regarding the general fruit-retribution (*vipāka-avaraṇa*), which are ordinarily interconnected.
Therefore, it is said that they are neither deep nor sharp.
These three phrases give rise to activity that is extraordinary;
they belong to the manifestation of the arousal of afflictions (*kleśa*).
When it arises, it is profound and heavy, impossible to restrain;
as it encounters objects, it increases further, beyond the power of any obstruction or control.
This is its characteristic of profundity.
They arise repeatedly, and whenever they do arise, they are profound and heavy;
therefore, they are called "sharp. Where there is sharpness but not depth, and depth but not sharpness, this principle may be applied accordingly to understand it.
As for the causes and conditions:
first, the seed as the cause of habituation;
second, the impelling action of karmic power.
Third, being stirred by the Māras:
those who practice have accumulated heavy afflictions throughout immeasurable kalpas.
The seeds of accomplishment perfume and continue in succession;
like a swift current of water, one does not perceive its rapidity while following it,
yet when one surveys it as a whole, one knows its rushing force.
The practitioner, following the flow of afflictions, drifts along the ocean of birth and death without any awareness at all; yet,
if they cultivate the factors of the path, they will go against the current of all existences.
Afflictions arise in towering profusion;
one must simply be diligent and exert oneself exceptionally, working through both day and night.
As for "action" (karma):
Having accumulated evil deeds over immeasurable eons, you are like one burdened by a debt or a grievance;
how could this possibly allow you to cultivate the path and attain liberation?
Therefore, your evil karma arises with great force.
It destroys contemplation of the mind,
preventing wholesome dharmas from being established,
like a river that appears calm and still while one fails to notice its underlying current.
A violent wind suddenly arose, and the waves were like a range of mountains.
If the sails had been let loose or the rudders broken, one would have perished in an instant;
however, by maintaining single-minded concentration, the boat was steered forward and backward, and they were saved.
As for Māra,
if one performs the deeds of Māra, one belongs to his subjects; therefore,
he cannot cause disturbance or confusion.
If one travels along the path and departs from this boundary to seek refuge in that,
the ten armies will seize and capture them; thus, the profound and sharp delusions will suddenly arrive,
like the waters of the great ocean which flow even without wind.
When the Magadhan dragon drinks up the water, all living beings flee toward it and cannot resist by force;
only by single-mindedly invoking the name of the Buddha can they escape.
To use fire as a metaphor: [the situation is likewise].
Shaking [the mind] is like the wind of habituation; fanning it is like the grease of karma; casting it [into the fire] is like Māra.
The activities of Māra are as explained below.
Contemplating the movement of afflictions through habituation is what is to be observed here.
Third, regarding the differences in the methods of treatment:
in the Hīnayāna, there are five methods of treatment,
which consist of both counteractive application and non-application.
These five together counteract the four types of afflictions that obstruct the Path;
their arising is as described in the section on the objects of karma, and so forth.
As for the antidotes:
Each category of affliction consists of three types,
totaling twelve; in correspondence with these,
there are likewise twelve [counteractive factors].
It is like setting up an array against an enemy;
this is called "counteracting" (*pratipakṣa*). As for "transformative counteracting" (*parivṛtti-pratipakṣa*):
Just as the contemplation of impurity is an antidote to desire but is not appropriate for one seeking liberation through pure observation, so too,
once one has attained release through pure contemplation and proceeds to cultivate a mind of loving-kindness,
how could one further inflict defilement and humiliation upon oneself by dwelling on foul things? How much more so when one is mindful of the peace and bliss of pure dharmas!
This is called transformative treatment (*parivṛtti-cikitsā*).
For one who is prone to anger, one teaches the meditation on impurity;
for one who is prone to delusion, one teaches the contemplation of the finite and the infinite.
For restlessness and distraction, one employs wisdom to discern them;
this is treating by turning [the mind] when it does not turn away from its illness.
All such cases are termed "treating by turning."
If both the medicine and the disease shift,
this is also called "shifting treatment";
it is likewise a counteractive treatment that is not a non-shifting treatment.
Although the illness may not improve despite treatment,
one should cultivate this method and treat solely with it;
because the illness does not improve even as the treatment is applied, it is called "treatment that does not turn back."
Regarding "treating combined [afflictions]":
when the illness is combined, the medicines must also be combined.
For example, if greed is combined with anger, one must employ the meditation on impurity together with compassion.
When there are one or two diseases, one also employs one or two medicines;
this is called concurrent treatment (*miśra-cikitsā*).
As for comprehensive treatment (*sarva-cikitsā*), one employs all the aforementioned methods together to treat a single disease.
This is called the Hīnayāna method, which first employs the five remedies and subsequently employs the knowledge of the truths (*satya-jñāna*) before attaining entry into the Real.
The Mahāyāna, however, clarifies that the remedy is neither oppositional nor cumulative, and so forth.
This is called the "treatment according to the ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha*).
Just as the agada medicine can cure all illnesses,
the Hinayana generally employs the three *siddhāntas* as its treatment.
In the Mahāyāna, the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint) is primarily employed as the remedy.
Within emptiness and non-arising, who is afflicted and who is the remedy?
Since afflictions themselves do not exist, what could possibly be transformed?
Since there is nothing that is transformed, nor is anything possessed simultaneously, it is simply by means of the single principle of non-arising that all things are universally treated.
This is extremely concise; one must skillfully grasp its intended meaning.
Regarding the fourth [section], the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā,
it likewise consists of ten points.
First, the exclusion of the object of conceptual thought:
At the very first moment a thought of desire arises, it is extremely subtle;
if one does not immediately restrain it, it will gradually increase,
leading to unrighteous conduct through the pull of craving for sensual matters.
Even down to the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes—
these are called the afflictions that give rise to the realm of hell.
Driven by the causes and conditions of desire, they lack a sense of shame and modesty, being coarse, arrogant, and defiant.
Lacking further propriety and righteousness, they lose the human lineage;
this is called being born into the realm of animals due to greed.
Furthermore, for the sake of the causes and conditions of desire, they are stingy and guard their possessions, and are likewise miserly toward the households of others.
This is called being born into the realm of hungry ghosts due to greed;
because of the causal conditions of desire, one gives rise to jealousy,
becoming suspicious and defensive, constantly seeking to surpass others.
To employ a hundred stratagems to ensnare and cause another to retreat in defeat is called being born into the realm of asuras due to greed.
Furthermore, because of the causes and conditions of desire, one deeply craves present pleasure and seeks marriage through formal rites.
Always practicing moderation and remaining in accord with benevolence and righteousness,
one observes the five precepts for the sake of future pleasures;
this is called being born in the human realm due to craving.
Furthermore, when the desire to arise— that base, coarse craving for celestial desires—
is countered by diligently cultivating the ten wholesome paths of action until they are pure and matured,
it will no longer arise spontaneously.
One contemplates that from the arising of desire, the six celestial realms are produced;
furthermore, one contemplates that by abandoning and reviling the desirous mind, one can give rise to pure meditative concentration,
which leads to the realms of the form heavens and the formless heavens.
Furthermore, one contemplates that desire is the origin;
since the origin brings forth suffering,
one becomes weary of this accumulation of suffering and cultivates the essential path of deliverance.
This is the realm of the śrāvakas.
If one contemplates that desire is ignorance, then by regarding desire as ignorance, the cycle of the formative forces (saṃskāra) is created without end;
if one brings desire to rest, then ignorance, the formative forces, and so forth, all come to rest.
This is the realm of the pratyekabuddhas.
If one contemplates desire as an obscuration and, giving rise to compassion, practices equanimity while fearing impermanence—
and so on, up to contemplating desire as delusion and the like.
This is the realm of the six perfections.
If one contemplates that desire is fundamentally unarisen,
neither abiding now nor destined to cease.
Desire itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is nirvāṇa;
this constitutes the realm of the Shared Teaching (p’unggyo).
Furthermore, one contemplates that the mind of desire possesses immeasurable characteristics.
Since the aggregates are neither one nor is suffering infinite,
one knows that the faculties, desires, and natures are all fully present due to the mind’s discrimination based on desire;
this constitutes the distinct teaching of the realms (*dhātu*).
The remaining three parts, wherein the afflictions give rise to all phenomena, are likewise so.
The sequential arising of all phenomena is termed the "object of discursive thought."
Regarding the inconceivable realm:
as it is said by the practitioner of non-action, "Lust is itself the Way; anger and delusion are likewise so."
Within these three dharmas, all Buddha-dharmas are fully contained.
Although these four parts are themselves the Path, they cannot, by following them one after another, lead a person toward the evil realms.
Furthermore, one must not sever what is not to be severed, for that would constitute overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Rather, it is called the Path when one does not sever delusion and craving, yet gives rise to various forms of clear knowledge and liberation (*vidyā-vimukti*).
One does not abide in discipline, nor does one abide in indiscipline.
To abide in indiscipline is the mark of a fool;
to abide in discipline is the dharma of the śrāvakas.
Why is this? Because ordinary persons are defiled by craving and follow along with the four parts [of existence];
thus, birth and death accumulate heavily, making them stubborn and difficult to tame.
Therefore, they are called "undisciplined.
Those of the Two Vehicles fear birth and death as if pursued by an enemy,
seeking to exit the triple world with haste.
An Arhat is called "the untamed.
Since the delusions of the three realms are exhausted, there are no further delusions to be tamed.
Thus, this state of being untamed is itself termed "taming."
A scorched seed does not sprout; once its root is destroyed, it is useless.
It is not so with the Bodhisattva, who possesses courage within the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra).
They do not relish nirvana;
they are courageous within birth-and-death, manifesting birth through non-birth,
and remain unsullied by the phenomena of birth.
It is like a flower in the mud, or like a physician treating an illness.
One does not relish nirvāṇa, and knowing that emptiness is neither empty nor non-empty, one is not realized by means of the dharma of emptiness.
It is like a bird flying through the sky, which does not dwell in the sky.
To enter nirvana without severing afflictions,
and to purify the sense faculties without abandoning the five desires—
this is precisely the intention of neither abiding in discipline nor abiding in indiscipline.
Now, when foolish people of the final age hear that the amra fruit is sweet and delicious to the taste,
they immediately crush its seed to taste it and find it extremely bitter;
thus, the sweet flavor of the fruit is entirely lost.
Because they lack wisdom, their excessive scrutiny is likewise like this.
Hearing that there is neither discipline nor non-discipline,
they are neither obstructed by discipline nor obstructed by non-discipline.
Because it is unobstructed, it is called the "unimpeded path" (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Because it is unimpeded, one becomes utterly licentious,
openly practicing what is unlawful without the slightest sense of shame.
This is no different from the behavior of birds and beasts.
This is a disease caused by excessive consumption of salt leading to parching thirst.
As the Sūtra says:
Those who are greedily attached to unimpeded dharmas are as far from the Buddha as heaven is from earth.
As the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra says:
To say, "I cultivate the signless," is not to cultivate the signless.
Such a person walks upon a non-path while desiring to penetrate the Buddha-way;
they instead obstruct themselves, becoming no different from the vulgar and base.
This is abiding in non-discipline, yet it is not non-abiding.
Furthermore, there are practitioners who, hearing that one neither abides in discipline nor abides in non-discipline,
fear both extremes and strive with great self-exertion to maintain themselves.
One who wishes to cultivate middle-way wisdom to sever and break through the two extremes cannot regard craving itself as the path; rather,
it is only after craving has been severed that one declares it to be the path.
This refers to abiding in a disciplined mind, not failing to abide therein.
The northern regions suffer from both of these faults.
Furthermore, among those who first study Madhyamaka, they are unable to gain benefit if they sever their desire for practice.
Relaxing your mind, you may engage in unwholesome conduct;
at first, such practice yields but a slight benefit.
From this point onward, however, you must continue to practice constantly without ceasing.
Furthermore, there is no further benefit in not changing one's conduct;
rather, having first benefited oneself, one transforms others and causes them to practice.
Moreover, he cites a sutra as proof.
Those who have received his transformation merely crave pleasure and delight, without the slightest benefit of the Path;
they rush headlong into indulgence until it becomes a prevailing custom,
thereby bringing disgrace upon the precepts and defiling the Triple Gem.
The collapse of the Zhou dynasty and the decline of the Buddha-dharma both originated from this.
This concerns abiding in non-discipline and abiding in discipline;
what has it to do with not abiding in either discipline or non-discipline?
This is called a great obstruction; what does it have to do with non-obstruction?
This is growth, not the Path; what does it have to do with the Buddha-path?
Thus, both the tamed and the untamed are called "untamed."
Why is this? Because all these are merely ordinary sentiments and not the conduct of the noble ones.
Now it is said:
He does not abide in discipline, nor does he abide in indiscipline;
he does not abide in that which is neither disciplined nor undisciplined;
he does not abide in both discipline and indiscipline.
They abide in both discipline and non-discipline;
they abide in neither discipline nor non-discipline;
and they abide in both discipline and non-discipline.
Why is this? Because afflictions are themselves emptiness, they do not abide in non-subjugation;
because afflictions are themselves the conventional, they do not abide in subjugation.
Because afflictions are themselves the Middle Way, one neither abides [in them], nor subdues them, nor fails to subdue them.
This is because one illuminates afflictions simultaneously.
Although one does not abide [in them], it is neither non-subduing nor non-non-subduing; for although one does not abide in subduing or non-subduing and so forth, [the Middle Way remains].
Yet they actually abide in states such as being disciplined or undisciplined;
although they actually abide in states such as being disciplined or undisciplined,
they do not actually abide in states such as being disciplined or undisciplined.
Why is this? Because one does not observe a single phrase in isolation;
a single phrase is itself all phrases.
Because all dharmas tend toward desire,
and because desire is the capital city of all dharmas;
apply this principle to every subsequent phrase.
That which is reckoned as the existence of desire is called "abiding in non-subjugation";
that which is reckoned as its non-existence is "abiding in subjugation.
Such things are explained with sovereign mastery, and so forth.
To thus realize its essence is called the path of non-obstruction.
All those who are unobstructed transcend birth and death by means of this single path.
How do they transcend?
At times, one realizes that desire is ultimately pure, free from burden and untainted,
like empty space; thus,
one emerges wide open from birth and death.
This is called abiding in the attainment of benefit through subduing.
At times, one may freely direct the mind to contemplate the causal conditions of this desire from beginning to end:
how many factors constitute the disease, and how many constitute the medicine?
Just as Viśuddhimat entered the limit of freedom from desire to liberate sentient beings,
when one performs this contemplation, one is suddenly liberated from birth and death.
This is called "abiding in the benefit of being untamed."
Sometimes benefit is gained because neither [of the two] is present;
sometimes benefit is gained by observing both.
Such skillful means regarding what should be dwelt upon and what should not be dwelt upon [is required].
Benefiting both oneself and others,
one does not diminish the bodhisattva-dharma,
exercising discernment through the four *siddhāntas*.
For example, when the monk Nandīndriya taught the Dharma of skillful means (*upāya*) to the lay devotees,
they all attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*);
yet the bhikṣu Viśeṣamati, practicing the Dharma of unskillful means, achieved nothing at all.
Later, while traveling through a village, he heard that the faculty of joy (*nandīndriya*) is itself the path to greed, hatred, and delusion.
How then can one preach to others the factors that obstruct the path?
Having performed the formal act of suspension (*pravāsanīyakarman*) against him, which was not yet finalized, the faculty of joy spoke this verse: [The verse follows.]
Even if they are already trapped within it,
the Bodhisattva knows that because they lack faith, they will inevitably fall into hell;
for this reason, he forcefully explains [the Dharma] to create the causes for future lives.
Skillfully observing the *siddhāntas*— whether concerning oneself or others, whether near or far—
and abiding in those who are disciplined or undisciplined,
one shall in all cases be free from error.
There is no fault whatsoever in not abiding in either discipline or indiscipline.
If one does not grasp the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*,
and if one abides in or does not abide [in these states], one weaves a net of craving for oneself and gives rise to the contempt and pride of others.
To be obstructed by oneself and to obstruct others is not non-obstruction.
If a single thought of affliction arises,
it fully encompasses the ten realms and one hundred dharmas without mutual hindrance.
Though many, they do not exist; though one, it is not non-existent.
The many do not accumulate, nor does the one disperse.
The many are not different from the one, nor is the one different from the many.
The many are each one, and each one is the many.
As the Sūtra says:
"In the darkness, the shadows of trees are not seen because they are dark."
The divine eye can see;
this is what is meant by having light within darkness.
The obstruction of wisdom is even more blind and dark than that.
This constitutes light existing within darkness,
just as a lamp and darkness may coexist; likewise,
light and darkness do not obstruct one another, nor do they destroy one another.
Why is this? It is because we see in the world that when a lamp is lit inside a room,
one does not know where the darkness has gone or reached.
If the lamp is extinguished, the nature of darkness returns;
yet its coming has no source, and its departure leaves no trace.
Since darkness is thus, [so too is all phenomena].
It is the same with light:
when one seeks darkness, no darkness is found, and light has nothing to destroy;
when one seeks light, no light is found, and darkness has nothing to obscure.
Although ignorance and darkness are clearly broken and the hindrances are dispelled,
one does not accept or cling to them;
not recollecting and not discriminating what newly arises is called "non-acceptance."
That which has arisen in the past is called non-attachment.
Not grasping internally is called non-recollection.
Not grasping externally is called non-discrimination.
Sublime wisdom is luminous and clear.
For this reason,
it is called "inconceivable," characterized by neither mutual obstruction nor mutual exclusion.
If the lamp of worldly wisdom is extinguished, the darkness of delusion will return;
if the light of Middle Way wisdom remains eternally still and unmoving,
it is like a divine jewel that constantly illuminates so that darkness does not come.
To contemplate the darkness of afflictions as the luminosity of great wisdom is to manifest the Bodhi of the Buddha; thus, delusions do not arise.
This may be understood by analogy with the aforementioned "Entry into the Realm of the Aggregates."
When observing in this way, one regrets one's own past transgressions and takes universal compassion for sentient beings. Why is this?
Because the principle is neither light nor dark.
Because of delusion, the darkness of the origin of suffering arises;
because of understanding the remedial Dharma, the light of the path and cessation emerges.
It is with reference to this darkness that compassion is felt.
Because it is based on clarity,
compassion arises simultaneously with its object;
because one seeks to fulfill the vow, one must establish the essential practice.
Among the essentials of practice, none precedes *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
To realize that the substance of the four categories of afflictions is itself empty is called "true cessation of substance," which is entry into the contemplation of emptiness.
To contemplate the dharmas of afflictions, medicines,
and diseases is called "stopping in accordance with conditions" (suiyuan zhi) and entering the contemplation of the provisional (jia guan).
To contemplate all afflictions as identical to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is [the contemplation of the ultimate].
This is called "stopping the two extremes and entering the Middle Way through contemplation.
By skillfully settling the mind and practicing these three modes of stopping and three modes of contemplation,
one achieves the single mind, the three eyes, and the three wisdoms.
If the eye of wisdom has not yet opened to pervasively shatter the hindrances,
one should contemplate the fourfold afflictions and the three provisionalities in every thought-moment;
neither from self, nor from others, nor from both together, nor apart from them, nor through the combination of single or multiple factors, do views and thoughts arise.
Knowing the illness and recognizing the medicine, ignorance does not arise.
Being neither true nor conditional, nescience does not arise.
Transversely and vertically, it is shattered and exhausted.
To discern suffering and its origin within emptiness itself is called knowing the obstruction;
to penetrate that very suffering and its origin as being emptiness is called knowing the penetration.
To construct [conceptual] illnesses out of the medicinal drugs of all phenomena is called knowing the obstructions;
to be able to know the medicine for all these ill phenomena is [knowing the remedies].
This is called knowing the penetration.
To invert the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and turn it into ignorance is called obstruction.
The transformation of ignorance into clarity is called penetration;
furthermore, one contemplates the afflictions while cultivating the factors of enlightenment.
When the fourfold mind arises, it immediately defiles the five aggregates.
One aggregate consists of immeasurable aggregates;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise immeasurable.
The aggregates are themselves emptiness;
they are merely the inverted, broken, and withered small trees of ordinary beings.
The aggregates are themselves the provisional.
The two vehicles perversely destroy the great flourishing tree;
they take the various aggregates (*skandhas*) as the Middle Way,
thereby abandoning and withering the teaching of flourishing.
With the cessation of the two extremes, one enters Great Nirvana;
even to the point of opening the three gates of liberation to enter the Cool Pond.
If obstructions are heavy, one should cultivate the auxiliary path.
Once the confusion and understanding are held in mutual balance, one should immediately seek support: when external desire arises, use the meditation on impurity as support;
when internal desire arises, use the meditations on repulsiveness as support;
when both internal and external desire arise, use the stages of mastery as support.
When anger arises in violation of the Dharma, assist it with loving-kindness toward sentient beings;
when anger arises in accordance with the Dharma, assist it with loving-kindness conditioned by phenomena;
when anger arises from conceptual proliferation, assist it with objectless loving-kindness.
The calculation of permanence and annihilation is assisted by the causal conditions of the three periods of time;
the calculation of self and person is assisted by the causal conditions of two periods of time;
the calculation of an inherent nature is assisted by the causal condition of a single thought-moment.
When a clear and sharp state of awareness arises, counting the breath serves as an aid.
When a dull and昏沉 (sinking) state of awareness arises, observing the breath serves as an aid.
When a state of awareness that is half-sunken and half-clear arises, following the breath serves as an aid.
Because the aids to the path are powerful, one is able to open the gate to nirvāṇa.
During the interval before it has opened, one may attain a certain kind of liberating insight or a certain kind of meditative concentration;
one should reflect upon this with mature deliberation.
Do not recklessly grasp at grasses, trees, tiles, or rubble, thinking they are lapis lazuli beads.
If you claim they are indeed such,
how could afflictions ever be extinguished?
Whether it be views, thoughts, afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, or ignorance—
none of these exist at all;
yet you erroneously claim they do, like the squeaking of a mouse.
If one says that "emptiness of emptiness" is like the emptiness of space or the emptiness of birds in flight,
yet has not recognized the successive stages of meditative practice and remains entirely unaligned with them,
then to presumptuously claim a higher rank is what constitutes an anomaly.
If internal or external obstacles arise, one should practice excellent patience (*kṣānti*).
If patience is not maintained, the bodhisattva will be ruined;
through unshakable patience, a sattva may achieve success.
One will immediately obtain the bestowed gift of Chan wisdom;
when obtaining this bestowal, do not give rise to attachment to dharmas,
for such attachment obstructs the true Way.
If one is free from falling back from the "Summit" stage, possessing sovereign mastery and unimpeded movement like the wind traveling through space,
one enters the stage of the copper wheel, destroys the delusions of ignorance, and achieves the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
One then obtains a great carriage— lofty, wide, and spacious— attended by a retinue of servants.
Riding upon this precious vehicle, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
This is called "the fourfold afflictions being fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas," and it is also called "traversing non-paths while penetrating the Buddha-path."
It is also called "afflictions are bodhi," and it is also called "entering nirvana without severing afflictions.
A detailed exposition contains thirty-six phrases.
One must first establish four propositions:
namely, not severing the afflictions and not entering nirvana.
To sever afflictions and enter nirvana;
to both sever and not sever, and both enter and not enter.
It is neither severed nor unsevered, neither entering nor non-entering.
The first phrase refers to ordinary worldlings;
the second refers to those beyond training (aśaikṣas).
The third refers to those in training (śaikṣa);
the fourth refers to that which is correct in principle.
These constitute the four fundamental propositions.
Each phrase opens up four aspects.
Regarding the four aspects of the first phrase:
they are non-interruption and non-entry.
It does not enter through cessation;
it does not enter through both cessation and non-cessation;
it does not enter through neither cessation nor non-cessation.
The first refers to ordinary worldlings who give rise to evil;
the second refers to non-Buddhists who have attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);
the third refers to non-Buddhists who have attained meditative concentration and given rise to [wrong] views.
The fourth refers to those who are indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Regarding the "four" in the subsequent phrase,
it refers to those who have entered cessation (nirodha-samāpanna).
Entry through non-interruption;
entry through both interruption and non-interruption;
and entry through neither interruption nor non-interruption.
The first refers to those who analyze phenomena (dharma) and are beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The second refers to those who realize the essence of phenomena and are beyond training.
The third refers to those who both analyze and realize the essence and are still in training (śaikṣa).
The latter refers to the profound merging with the principle of truth;
this is precisely "entry.
As for the third set of four phrases:
Both severed and not severed, both entered and not entered;
severed yet entered and not entered;
not severed yet entered and not entered.
It is neither severed nor not severed, and it both enters and does not enter.
The first refers to those practitioners who analyze the substance;
the second refers to those practitioners who analyze phenomena; the third refers to those practitioners who realize the nature of reality.
The fourth refers to the truth common to both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Regarding the fourth set of four propositions:
it is neither abandoned nor not abandoned, and neither entered nor not entered.
Neither abandoning nor not abandoning, neither entering nor not entering;
neither abandoning nor not abandoning, neither entering nor not entering;
both abandoning and not abandoning, neither entering nor not entering.
The first refers to the principle common to both ordinary beings and sages;
the second refers to the principle of analytical wisdom (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding phenomena;
the third refers to the principle of intrinsic nature (dharmatā) regarding phenomena.
The fourth refers to the principle of the practitioner who analyzes the substance (*dravya*).
This is explained through sixteen phrases;
when combined with the four fundamental phrases, these twenty phrases lead one into *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, sixteen phrases emerge from the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Regarding the first four fundamental phrases:
they refer to not severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) and not emerging into *nirvāṇa*.
One abandons afflictions and emerges into nirvāṇa;
one both abandons and does not abandon afflictions,
and both emerges and does not emerge.
Neither severed nor not severed;
neither emerged nor not emerged.
For each individual phrase there are four permutations; the first four permutations are as follows:
Not severing the afflictions, one does not emerge from nirvāṇa;
severing the afflictions, one emerges from nirvāṇa;

neither severing nor not severing the afflictions, one both emerges and does not emerge from nirvāṇa; neither severing nor not severing the afflictions, one neither emerges nor does not emerge from nirvāṇa.
The first refers to those of the Two Vehicles who realize the nature of phenomena;
the second refers to Bodhisattvas who realize the nature of phenomena and emerge into the provisional;
the third refers to Bodhisattvas who realize that the nature of phenomena is both empty and provisional.
The fourth refers to the reality of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Regarding the second set of four propositions:
it is the emergence through the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*).
The severing of afflictions is not emerging;
the severing of afflictions is both emerging and not emerging;
the severing of afflictions is neither emerging nor not emerging.
First, those who analyze phenomena and are of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), assisting the Buddha to benefit sentient beings;
second, those who analyze phenomena and are of the stage of no-more-learning who immediately enter cessation (*nirvāṇa*);
third, those who analyze phenomena and are of the stage of learning (*śaikṣa*) who benefit both themselves and others.
The fourth refers to the Truth.
Regarding the third set of four propositions:
it is both severed and not severed, and both emerged and not emerged.
It is both severed and not severed, yet it emerges;
it is both severed and not severed, yet it does not emerge;
it is both severed and not severed, neither emerging nor not emerging.
The first phrase refers to Bodhisattvas who employ the analytical method of the essence (*tattva-vibhāga*) to enter emptiness;
the second phrase refers to Bodhisattvas who employ the analytical method of the essence to emerge into the provisional (*upāya-niṣkrama*);
the third phrase refers to those of the Two Vehicles who employ the analytical method of the essence.
The four propositions refer to the principle of the essence of phenomena merging with the truth.
Regarding the fourth set of four propositions:
it is neither severed nor not severed, neither emerging nor not emerging.
It is neither through cessation nor non-cessation that there is emergence;
it is neither through cessation nor non-cessation that there is non-emergence;
it is neither through cessation nor non-cessation that there is both emergence and non-emergence.
The first phrase refers to those who realize the principle (*tattva*).
The second phrase refers to Bodhisattvas who realize phenomena (*dharma*) and emerge into the conventional world.
The third phrase refers to the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) who realize phenomena.
The four phrases refer to the bodhisattvas who enter emptiness by means of the essential nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
If one were to establish two fundamental sets of eight phrases for each of the "entering" and "emerging," they would constitute forty phrases in total.
If the fundamental [categories] are combined into four propositions,
they constitute thirty-six propositions.
Question:
Question: Do the thirty-six *śamatha* practices belong only to the Tripitaka and the Shared [Vehicles], or can they also be categorized as Distinct and Perfect?
Answer: [They can.]
The essence of the Dharma’s meaning is all-encompassing;
if one were to explain it further in detail,
one would distinguish it according to the four gates of the Separate and Perfect Teachings.
Regarding the four fundamental propositions:
"non-interruption" refers to not entering the gate of emptiness;
"interruption" refers to entering the gate of existence.
It is both severed and not severed; it both enters and does not enter.
It is both empty and possesses gates.
It is neither severed nor not severed; it neither enters nor does not enter.
This is precisely the gate of neither emptiness nor existence.
Regarding the four further [aspects] for each individual gate:
"neither abandoning nor entering" is the world-siddhānta.
"Neither ceasing nor entering" is the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint for people).
"Neither ceasing nor entering, yet also entering" is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic counteraction).
"Neither ceasing nor neither entering nor not entering" is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth).
Furthermore, within one gate, one may again establish four gates.
That is to say: "neither ceasing nor entering" refers to the gate of emptiness;
"ceasing but not entering" refers to the gate of existence.
Neither ceasing, it both enters and does not enter;
this refers to being both empty and having gates.
Neither ceasing, it neither enters nor does not enter.
This refers to the gate that is neither empty nor existent.
Since this one gate can be understood,
the other three gates may likewise be understood through their respective distinctions by analogy.
Since entry into nirvāṇa by way of the four gates is thus, how are the sixteen gates of emergence from nirvāṇa? They are:
non-interruption and non-emergence.
It is not non-emergent;
it is neither non-emergent nor emergent;
it is neither non-emergent nor non-non-emergent.
The first refers to the gate of emptiness;
the second refers to the gate of existence;
the third refers to the gate of both emptiness and existence.
The fourth refers to the gate of neither emptiness nor existence.
The four propositions of one gate are thus;
the remaining three gates can be understood accordingly.
The thirty-six and forty [categories] may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
This, then, is the principle of universally encompassing both the small and the great through the analysis of their substance.
If one grasps this meaning, it should likewise apply to all phenomena by way of analogy.
Question:
If one contemplates the Buddha,
nirvāṇa, and prajñā according to the Dharma.
These three are of one single characteristic.
Since the thirty-six phrases have already clarified *nirvāṇa*,
what further can be said regarding *prajñā*?
Answer:
If nirvana is already identical to prajñā,
why wait to ask further?
Now I shall explain further: all dharmas give rise to prajñā, and prajñā does not arise;
all dharmas both give rise to it and do not give rise to it.
Prajñā is both arising and non-arising;
all phenomena are neither arising nor non-arising;
Prajñā is neither arising nor non-arising.
This is the fundamental fourfold statement.
To further divide the first phrase into four:
all phenomena arise, and prajñā arises.
Whether all phenomena arise, Prajñā does not arise;
whether all phenomena arise, Prajñā both arises and does not arise;
whether all phenomena arise, Prajñā neither arises nor does not arise.

The first phrase refers to the arising of the *prajñā* of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) from conventional objects; the second refers to the arising of the *prajñā* of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) from conventional objects;
the third refers to the simultaneous arising of both types of *prajñā* from conventional objects.
The fourth refers to the prajñā of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) arising from conventional objects.
Regarding the second set of four propositions:
the non-arising of all phenomena does not give rise to the non-arising of prajñā.
All phenomena are non-arising, yet prajñā arises;
all phenomena are non-arising, yet prajñā both arises and does not arise;
all phenomena are non-arising, yet prajñā neither arises nor does not arise.
The first phrase refers to the true object giving rise to the *prajñā* of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
The second phrase refers to the true object giving rise to the *prajñā* of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).
The third phrase refers to the true object giving rise to both types of *prajñā* simultaneously.
The fourfold statement refers to the wisdom of the Middle Way that arises from the true realm;
the third fourfold statement refers to the fact that all phenomena both arise and do not arise.
Prajñā both arises and does not arise;
all dharmas both arise and do not arise.
Prajñā arises.
All phenomena both arise and do not arise;
yet Prajñā does not arise.
All phenomena both arise and do not arise.
Prajñā is neither arising nor non-arising.
Regarding the first phrase, two objects simultaneously give rise to two types of wisdom.
Second, the two objects together give rise to conventional wisdom (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
The third refers to both objects jointly giving rise to true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*).
The fourth refers to both objects jointly giving rise to intermediate knowledge (*madhyamajñāna*).
Regarding the fourth set of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
All phenomena are neither born nor unborn;
Prajñā is neither born nor unborn. Since all phenomena are neither born nor unborn, Prajñā is born.
All phenomena are neither born nor unborn.
Prajñā is unborn, yet all phenomena are neither born nor unborn; prajñā is both born and unborn. The former refers to the arising of middle-level wisdom from the middle-level object.
The second refers to the arising of conventional knowledge from a neutral object;
the third refers to the arising of ultimate knowledge from a neutral object;
the fourth refers to the simultaneous arising of both types of knowledge from a neutral object.
The sixteen phrases have now been fully explained.
Next, it is taught that while the arising of all phenomena is born of prajñā,
the non-arising of all phenomena is also born of prajñā.
Prajñā gives rise to all phenomena; it both arises and does not arise.
Prajñā gives rise to all phenomena; it neither arises nor does not arise.
The former refers to the wisdom of the path (mārga-jñāna) illuminating the conventional realm.
The second refers to path-knowledge illuminating the true realm;
the third refers to path-knowledge illuminating both realms;
the fourth refers to path-knowledge illuminating the middle realm.
Next, it is explained that when prajñā is non-arising, all phenomena are non-arising; when prajñā is non-arising, all phenomena are arising;
and when prajñā is non-arising, all phenomena are both arising and non-arising.
Prajñā does not give rise to any phenomena; they are neither arising nor non-arising.
This clarifies the meaning of true wisdom illuminating all objects;
it may be understood according to what was explained previously.
Next, it is explained that *prajñā* both arises and does not arise, opening up four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
This clarifies how the true wisdom of the *mārgākāra* (aspects of the path) and so forth illuminates the four objects, and so forth.
Next, it is explained that *prajñā* neither arises nor does not arise.
The wisdom of the Middle Way illuminates the four objects, as can be known from the detailed exposition.
These constitute the sixteen [aspects].
Taken together with the fundamental [aspects], they form thirty-six propositions.
Question:
Furthermore, what is the dharma-body?
Answer:
Since Prajñā is itself the Dharmakāya, what need is there for further questioning?
If one wishes to analyze it, it can be understood through the mind;
there is no need for prolixity in the text.
Furthermore, the four bodies—the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, the Response-body, and the Transformation-body—are the foundation.
From each of these bodies, four bodies arise;
that is to say, from the Dharma-body arises the Reward-body.
One should give rise to the transformations that ought to be produced;
all three types of arising are complete.
It is the same for the remaining bodies as well.
These constitute sixteen bodies.
Furthermore, one enters from four bodies into one body;
it is the same for each and every body.
There are another sixteen;
together with the preceding fundamental ones, these constitute thirty-six bodies.
Each and every body is the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, both are able to arise;
therefore, both are able to enter, and so forth.
○ Third, regarding the contemplation of the object of illness:
Indeed, to possess a body is itself a disease;
it is like four snakes of differing natures,
or like water and fire which are mutually opposed.
Owls and owlets nest together; pythons and mice share the same burrow.
It is a vessel of poison, a heavy burden, and a thicket of all sufferings.
With the four kingdoms as neighbors, they mutually invade and destroy one another.
"When strengths are equal, there is temporary harmony; when one rides upon emptiness, there is annexation.
This analogy can be understood through the alternation of the four elements' flourishing and decline.
Thus it is said in the *Dharmaparyāya-saṃpraśna*.
May you have little illness and little affliction.
The Buddha shares the same nature as humans;
since humans are subject to illness, it cannot be absent from him by his own power.
It is merely said to be slight.
There are two meanings of "sickness":
first, actual sickness within the causal stage.
Second is the provisional illness manifested atop the [two] fruits.
If one lies prostrate in Vaiśālī, feigning illness to give rise to the teaching,
one uses this physical ailment to instruct the common people, disparaging the Small Vehicle and censuring the Great.

Thereupon, together with Mañjuśrī, he extensively elucidated the three kinds of subduing through illness as the cause, and extensively elucidated the four kinds of consolation regarding illness as the fruit.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata, by means of the metaphor of extinction, spoke of permanence; by means of the illness, he spoke of power.
All of these are skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) for entering the gates of the Dharma to lead away those afflicted by illness;
such provisional illnesses are not what is being examined here.
What is being examined now is the body born of karmic retribution.
The movements of the four snakes cause one to neglect the cultivation of the Noble Path;
if one can observe them, it will further increase one's application of the mind.
Those of superior wisdom and keen faculties understand this and abide in patience.
Thus, regarding the object of illness, one attains thorough penetration without the need for further elaboration;
however, for those who do not yet understand, I shall now provide a further analysis.
It is like felling a great tree: with ten thousand axes, it falls at once.
It is like carving a massive rock; it is only after hundreds of millions of strikes that it is finally pierced.
Therefore, this is stated repeatedly. Now, chronic illness and long journeys are great obstacles to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
If the body is afflicted by disease, one loses the merit already cultivated and incurs immeasurable demerit.
The Sūtra says:
"To destroy the life-preserving float and to pull down the bridge is to lose right mindfulness.
Because of illness, one violates the precepts as if destroying the life-preserving float."
To destroy meditative concentration is like pulling down a bridge;
to give rise to perverse and inverted thoughts, to cherish this foul body of pus and blood, and to destroy the pure Dharma-body is called the loss of right mindfulness.
For this reason, [it is so named].

One should further contemplate the object of the patient: suppose there is a person who, when healthy, is indolent and lingers about with negligence; yet when illness strikes urgently, they apply themselves with renewed vigor and is able to accomplish various tasks.
Furthermore, as capacities and conditions differ, awakening should occur within the context of illness;
that is, one must encounter the realm of illness as the causal condition for the four *siddhāntas*.
Contemplating illness is fivefold.
First, clarifying the characteristics of illness;
second, the causes and conditions for the arising of illness;
third, the methods of treatment.
Fourth, the decrease and increase;
fifth, the clarification of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
First, regarding the characteristics of illness:
If one is a skilled physician who understands the four great elements well:
the superior physician listens to the voice;
the middling physician examines the complexion.
Regarding the physician of lower grade who examines the pulse:
at present, there is no need for precise mastery of medical methods; it suffices to have a general understanding.
Indeed, the principles of the pulse are integral to the Way of Medicine and cannot be said to be fully exhaustive.
A brief indication of the symptoms of the five viscera:
if the pulse is full and straight, it is the symptom of liver disease;
if it is light and floating, it is the symptom of heart disease.
A sharp, piercing pulse indicates a lung disorder;
one like a string of beads indicates a kidney disorder;
and one that is heavy and slow indicates a spleen disorder.
The details are as explained in the *Śarīrāsthisamudgaka-sūtra*.
If the body is heavy with suffering,
characterized by firm knots and piercing pain, [one should apply the following].
Emaciation due to withered paralysis is the characteristic sign of a great disorder of the earth element;
if there is hollow swelling and bloating, this is the characteristic sign of a great disorder of the water element.
If the entire body feels intensely hot and the joints ache,
and one becomes suddenly exhausted with labored breathing,
these are the signs of a disorder of the fire element.
If the mind is suspended, vacant, and dazed,
or if one is distressed and experiences forgetfulness,
these are the signs of a wind disorder (vāta).
Furthermore, a lack of luster on the face and the absence of perspiration on the hands and feet are signs of liver disease.
A greenish or pale complexion on the face is a sign of heart disease.
A dark complexion on the face is a sign of disease in the lungs.
A lack of physical strength is a sign of disease in the kidneys.
A body feeling rough like wheat chaff is a sign of disease in the spleen.
If there is a white substance upon the liver, it causes the eyes to ache, the blood vessels to become dilated and form white opacities,
or the eyes to become cracked, or sores to develop above or below them,
or tears to flow upon exposure to wind and cold.
There may be itching or piercing pain;
the eyes may appear sunken, and one becomes prone to anger upon encountering various matters.
This disease arises because the lungs have harmed the liver.
It may be treated by using exhaled breath.
If the heart feels parched with heat while the hands and feet are cold to the touch,
the heart is oppressed, strength is diminished, and the lips and mouth are dry and cracked.
A mass forms below the navel; hot food cannot be ingested,
cold food causes heartburn, dizziness, and distress, while one is prone to sleepiness, forgetfulness,
and swelling of the heart region.
Dizziness, stammering speech, and tension in the shoulder blades;
the four limbs ache with distress, the heart is exhausted, and the body feels a steaming heat,
resembling the symptoms of malaria.
Or it may cause internal knots or dropsy, such that one sees objects close at hand as if through coarse cloth or silk, yet cannot see what is distant.
This is the kidneys harming the heart; it can be treated by means of blowing and chanting.
If there is distension of the lungs and obstruction of the chest, with pain beneath both flanks,
aching in both shoulder blades as if carrying a heavy burden,
stiffness in the head and neck, and coarse, labored breathing.
Only air exits, none enters;
sores break out over the entire body;
the throat itches as if with insects, making it impossible to swallow or spit out; or sores may develop in the throat and the jaw becomes locked.
Alternatively, wind may be provoked,
causing pus and blood to flow from the nostrils, darkness of vision, pain in the nasal bridge,
the growth of fleshy tissue within the nose, obstruction of the breath, and the inability to distinguish between fragrant and foul odors.
This mind harms the lungs and causes illness;
or, it may cause illness through the conflict of drinking cold water while eating hot food.
One may treat this by exhaling breath.
If the hundred vessels do not flow, there will be pain in every joint;
the body will swell, the ears will become deaf, the nose will be congested, and the lower back will ache.
The spine will feel stiff, and the chest and abdomen will be distended and full.
There is labored breathing, congestion in the chest, heaviness in the four limbs,
a dark and emaciated complexion, urgency and pain in the bladder, distress,
or urinary frequency and obstruction of the urethra, with the feet and knees becoming cold and numb.
This spleen harms the kidneys.
Furthermore, its disease-demon resembles the Lord of the Hearth;
it has neither head nor face and comes once to seize people.
It may be treated by using the Qi of the Liver.
If there is itching and a pricking sensation on the face and body, or generalized itching and a sense of oppression,
this is the Liver harming the Spleen.
Its color may appear like a basket or like a child striking a wooden drum;
it may also swirl and rotate like a whirlwind.
This can be treated by using the *yā* breath.
Furthermore, if there is excessive drowsiness, it is because the *hun* soul is lacking in the liver;
if there is excessive forgetfulness of what precedes and follows, it is because the *shen* spirit is lacking in the heart;
if there is excessive terror and epilepsy, [it is due to the lack of the *po* soul in the lungs].
This means that there is no *po* (spiritual essence) within the lungs;
if one laughs excessively out of grief,
this means there is no *zhi* (willpower) within the kidneys.
If there is much delusion and confusion,
this is because the spleen lacks intentionality;
if there is much despondency and resentment, it is likewise.
Within these aggregates there is no essence;
this is called the characteristic of the illness of the six spirits.
Second, it clarifies that there are six causes and conditions for the arising of illness.
First, illness arises because the four great elements are in disharmony;
second, illness arises because of irregularity in diet;
third, illness arises because of lack of balance in seated meditation.
Fourth, malevolent spirits find an opportunity; fifth, it is caused by the deeds of Māra;
sixth, illness arises from the activation of karma.
These are the instances where the four great elements are not in harmony.

This applies even to cases of red dysentery, white dysentery,

The face is bluish;
the eyes are rolled back;

As for the method for those who do not distinguish [the specific ailment]: press the *dantian* with the hand with firm pressure;
it will be cured in a short while.
Furthermore, wherever there is a painful spot on the body,
one strikes that sick spot with a hand-held staff forty or fifty times.
What is the intention behind this?
Indeed, there is no illness that is not produced by the mind.
When the mind harbors sorrow, grief, or anxious deliberation, malevolent influences gain entry.
Now, being constrained by this pain, one has no leisure for frivolous thoughts.
When the deviant energies depart, the illness is eliminated.
Regarding the four clarifications of decrease and increase,
both decrease and increase occur through both gradual and sudden means.
If one employs the breath excessively such that the five viscera suddenly overturn,
then even if they have not yet fully overturned, the condition will gradually progress toward intensification.
As for those who achieve sudden transformation:
if a person skillfully practices and experiences a sudden, expansive benefit,
then even while contending with the illness, [the remedy] will prevail.
Regarding those who will gradually recover later on:
it is like taking medicinal decoctions, where one only begins to reap the benefits after months or years have passed;
internal treatment is likewise so.
If the faculties of the mind are sharp and the afflictions are light, or if the faculties are sharp but the afflictions are heavy;
or if the faculties are dull and the afflictions are light, or if the faculties are dull and the afflictions are heavy—
these differences give rise to the distinctions between gradual and sudden [attainment].
Now, worldly medicine requires great expenditure of wealth and labor;
it is bitter and difficult to ingest, with many prohibitions.
Those who cherish their lives and fear death will take it as their final recourse.
Now, without spending a single coin and without wasting even half a day’s labor,
one may indulge in eating and drinking at will, free from the worry of bitter tastes.
Yet no one is willing to practice it.
The mediocre do not distinguish between goods;
when the tone is lofty, those who harmonize with it are few.
I am deeply grieved by this.
If one can fulfill ten dharmas, there will certainly be a positive result.
The first is faith.
Second is function,
up to the tenth consciousness which acts as an obstruction;
faith is the source of the Way.
The initial gateway to the Buddha-dharma is like a leper who believes blood to be milk,

One must resolutely believe that this Dharma can cure this illness and not give rise to doubt;
for to believe yet not apply it to oneself is of no benefit.
It is like grasping a sharp sword but not using it to strike a thief;
instead, one is harmed by it.
Not using [the Dharma] is likewise so.
For what purpose is diligence required?
One must apply oneself with single-minded concentration during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, as well as in the morning and evening,
until one reaches the point where perspiration breaks out.
Just as it is difficult to obtain fire from wood that has been drilled but where the spark has ceased,
so it is with those who lack diligence.
What, then, is meant by "constancy"?
One should constantly employ remedial methods, remaining focused on the object of meditation at every moment without becoming distracted or agitated.
What are the specific ailments?
Specific ailments arise as previously described.
If one does not recognize the illness and applies treatments haphazardly without addressing the specific condition,
it will be of no benefit to the matter. What,
then, is meant by "expedient means" (upāya)?
Skillfully employing the methods of treatment for vomiting and constipation as appropriate,
one achieves success through mental cultivation without missing the proper timing,
just as one adjusts the tension of lute strings by turning the pegs and bridges.
When the sounds and rhythms of the light and heavy finger-movements are properly adjusted,
what is meant by "long duration"? It refers to the state where,
even after prolonged practice, no further benefit is gained.
Without regard for days or months, one practices without ceasing or abandoning.
What is meant by "knowing what to adopt and what to discard"?
That which is beneficial is diligently employed; that which is detrimental is corrected and reformed.
What is meant by "knowing how to protect"?
It means being well-attentive to prohibitions and regulations regarding movement and diet so as not to cause contact with them.
What is meant by "recognizing obstructions"?
If it is beneficial, do not speak of it with disdain; if it is not yet beneficial, do not harbor doubt or slander.
When speaking to others, whether it is incorrect or correct, once it has become incorrect, it will manifest further.
If treated further, it will not be cured;
even if it were to improve, the effort required would be double.
However, if one can fulfill ten dharmas, [it will be healed].
By employing these aforementioned remedies, the benefit to your concentration will be certain beyond doubt.
I shall stand as your guarantor for this matter;
it shall never prove false.
